title: Greg Ashman's Journey to Misrepresenting Hattie Allegations
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Stephen Vainker responds to Greg Ashman's repeated public mischaracterizations of Vainker's case against John Hattie, documenting four specific ways Ashman has misled his audience about the substantive evidence of research misconduct. Vainker's core complaint is that Ashman continues to describe the allegations as merely unproven and untested despite: (1) Hattie himself thanking Vainker for finding a non-existent reference in his work; (2) a formal university investigation finding errors in Hattie's database, citation practices, and opening a plagiarism inquiry; and (3) the preliminary investigation letter acknowledging 'unintended errors' and recommending improved citation practices. Vainker identifies four distortions in Ashman's public commentary: overplaying a single minor error Vainker made in one tweet as evidence that 'a few' of Vainker's points were wrong; placing responsibility for Hattie's legal action on Vainker rather than recognizing it as strategic suppression of settled findings; describing Hattie's inclusion of non-existent references as still merely 'allegations'; and implying Vainker has only accused Hattie of minor citation errors rather than direct, serious plagiarism (copying without attribution). Vainker frames the broader problem as a structural dilemma: on one side, a complacent and incompetent educational academia; on the other, social media edu-celebrities driven by the attention economy rather than genuine truth-seeking. He argues that Ashman's uninformed interventions exemplify how easily the drive for social media engagement can displace rigorous engagement with evidence in education discourse.
points: The status of Vainker's allegations is not merely claimed but partially confirmed: Hattie personally acknowledged at least one non-existent reference, the university formally investigated and found database errors, and the pro vice-chancellor wrote acknowledging 'unintended errors' and inadequate citation practices — none of which is consistent with treating the case as a set of unproven claims.

Ashman's framing of Hattie's legal action as having a 'certain inevitability' given Vainker's error treats a strategic use of litigation to suppress settled findings as if it were a reasonable scholarly response to a factual dispute — inverting the power dynamic between a whistleblower and a well-resourced target.

The charge that Vainker has only made allegations about less serious forms of plagiarism is directly refuted by Vainker's published record: the most serious allegations — copying without any attribution — are precisely the ones he documented in detail, and the most serious are the ones the university found sufficient grounds to formally investigate.

Ashman's career pattern, as Vainker describes it, is one of building social media authority by taking on prominent figures without engaging substantively with evidence — the attack on Oliver Caviglioli being an example of content-free positioning that nonetheless generated attention.

The systemic problem Vainker identifies is structural: education research integrity sits between an ineffective institutional accountability mechanism (universities) and an attention-economy-driven influencer culture that prioritizes engagement over truth — and the Hattie case exposes what happens when both fail simultaneously.
quotes: My case against John Hattie is far from unproven allegations. Hattie himself has thanked me for finding a non-existent reference in his work. The preliminary university investigation, whatever its flaws, found errors in his database and citation practices and saw it fit to formally investigate his plagiarism.

Having taken a position against me on the basis of one poorly worded tweet I made two years ago, Ashman has not noticed that the facts of the case have long passed him by. Having built up his career largely outside the university, Ashman appears at times to be driven by the imperatives of the attention economy to lead the educational culture wars rather than engaging in a genuine search for truth amongst a community of scholars.

No. It is a settled fact that in Hattie's work 'there's research that he's referenced that doesn't really exist'. Hattie even thanked me for finding it. Whether or not this constitutes an AI hallucination or not depends on whether you can find any substance in this rather ridiculous defence based on the existence of various 'drafts'.

It is ridiculous for Ashman to hold me responsible for the legal action, saying that on the basis of the above error there was 'a certain inevitability' of the legal case. Hattie's legal action is self-evidently hollow and strategic, aimed at preventing amplification of my claims. Hattie has never publicly said what precisely in my work is incorrect or defamatory, despite the huge volume of my claims against him.

The strong implication is that I have not accused Hattie of the more serious form of plagiarism — directly lifting people's work without citing them at all. That's not true, I can assure Ashman that a lot of the plagiarism I have shown Hattie committed was 'really, really bad'.

In the scheme of things, Ashman's uninformed interventions will have very little impact on what happens with the Hattie case. But they do help show us that we're somewhat awkwardly positioned, if not stuck, between a rock and a hard place: a complacent, unfocused, and incompetent educational academia on the one side, and social media edu-celebrities on the other.
It is all too easy to drift away from a focus on guiding education research towards integrity, and ultimately towards meaningfully improving schools.
